questions.q: What is the closest star to Earth?
questions.fact: The Sun is about 150 million kilometers away, much closer than any other star.

questions.q: Which star is the closest to our Sun?
questions.fact: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away, so its light takes over four years to reach us.

questions.q: What is the brightest star in the night sky?
questions.fact: Sirius is nicknamed the Dog Star because it sits in the constellation Canis Major, the Great Dog.

questions.q: Which star stays almost still in the sky above Earth's North Pole?
questions.fact: Polaris, the North Star, has helped travelers find north for hundreds of years.

questions.q: What two gases make up most of the Sun?
questions.fact: About three quarters of the Sun's mass is hydrogen.

questions.q: What process makes the Sun shine?
questions.fact: In the Sun's core, hydrogen atoms smash together to make helium and release huge amounts of energy.

questions.q: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
questions.fact: If the Sun suddenly vanished, we would not notice for about 8 minutes.

questions.q: What type of star is the Sun?
questions.fact: Even though it is called a dwarf, the Sun is bigger than most stars in the Milky Way.

questions.q: What is the visible surface of the Sun called?
questions.fact: The photosphere is about 5,500 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: What is the Sun's thin outer atmosphere, seen glowing during a total solar eclipse, called?
questions.fact: The corona is over a million degrees, far hotter than the Sun's surface, and scientists are still studying why.

questions.q: What are the darker, cooler patches on the Sun's surface called?
questions.fact: Sunspots are caused by strong magnetic fields, and some are bigger than Earth.

questions.q: What happens during a solar eclipse?
questions.fact: A total solar eclipse can turn day into twilight for a few minutes.

questions.q: What happens during a lunar eclipse?
choices: Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
The Moon passes behind the Sun
questions.fact: During a total lunar eclipse the Moon often turns a coppery red, which is why people call it a blood moon.

questions.q: Why does the Moon shine at night?
questions.fact: The Moon's surface is actually a dark gray, a bit like old asphalt.

questions.q: About how long does the Moon take to orbit Earth?
questions.fact: The Moon takes about 27.3 days to orbit Earth, but about 29.5 days to go from one full moon to the next.

questions.q: Why do we always see the same side of the Moon?
choices: It does not spin at all
It spins once for each trip around Earth
The other side is too dark to see
questions.fact: This is called tidal locking, and many moons in the solar system do it.

questions.q: What are the big, flat, dark areas on the Moon called?
questions.fact: Early astronomers thought these dark plains were seas, so they named them maria, which is Latin for seas.

questions.q: Which mission was the first to land people on the Moon?
questions.fact: Apollo 11 landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969.

questions.q: Who was the second person to walk on the Moon?
questions.fact: Buzz Aldrin stepped onto the Moon about 19 minutes after Neil Armstrong.

questions.q: Which Apollo 11 astronaut stayed in orbit around the Moon while the others landed?
questions.fact: Michael Collins flew the command module Columbia alone around the Moon.

questions.q: What was the name of the Apollo 11 lunar module that landed on the Moon?
questions.fact: When it touched down, Neil Armstrong radioed that the Eagle has landed.

questions.q: Which Apollo mission had an oxygen tank explode on the way to the Moon?
questions.fact: The crew could not land, but they looped around the Moon and made it home safely.

questions.q: How many people have walked on the Moon?
questions.fact: Twelve astronauts walked on the Moon during six Apollo missions between 1969 and 1972.

questions.q: Which Apollo mission was the last to land on the Moon?
questions.fact: Apollo 17 landed in December 1972, and no one has walked on the Moon since.

questions.q: Which mission was the first to carry astronauts around the Moon?
questions.fact: The Apollo 8 crew took the famous Earthrise photo on Christmas Eve 1968.

questions.q: What did astronauts drive on the Moon during the last three Apollo missions?
questions.fact: The three lunar rovers were left behind and are still parked on the Moon.

questions.q: Which country launched the first artificial satellite?
questions.fact: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1 on October 4, 1957, starting the Space Race.

questions.q: What was the name of the dog that orbited Earth aboard Sputnik 2 in 1957?
questions.fact: Laika was a stray dog from the streets of Moscow.

questions.q: Who was the first woman to travel into space?
questions.fact: Valentina Tereshkova orbited Earth 48 times aboard Vostok 6 in 1963.

questions.q: Who was the first American woman in space?
questions.fact: Sally Ride flew aboard the Space Shuttle Challenger in 1983.

questions.q: Who was the first American to orbit Earth?
questions.fact: John Glenn circled Earth three times in Friendship 7 in 1962.

questions.q: Who was the first American to travel into space?
questions.fact: Alan Shepard later hit golf balls on the Moon during Apollo 14.

questions.q: Who was the first person to go on a spacewalk?
questions.fact: Alexei Leonov floated outside his spacecraft for about 12 minutes in 1965.

questions.q: What was the name of Yuri Gagarin's spacecraft?
questions.fact: Yuri Gagarin's flight on April 12, 1961, lasted about 108 minutes.

questions.q: What does NASA stand for?
questions.fact: NASA studies flight in the air (aeronautics) as well as space.

questions.q: In what year was NASA created?
questions.fact: NASA was created in 1958, less than a year after Sputnik 1 launched.

questions.q: Which space station have astronauts lived on without a break since the year 2000?
questions.fact: People have lived on the International Space Station continuously since November 2000.

questions.q: About how long does the International Space Station take to circle Earth once?
questions.fact: That means astronauts on board see about 16 sunrises every day.

questions.q: About how high above Earth does the International Space Station orbit?
questions.fact: That is roughly the distance from New York City to Washington, DC.

questions.q: About how fast does the International Space Station travel?
questions.fact: At that speed, it could cross the whole United States in about 10 minutes.

questions.q: Which Soviet and Russian space station orbited Earth from 1986 to 2001?
questions.fact: Mir means peace or world in Russian.

questions.q: What was the name of America's first space station, launched in 1973?
questions.fact: Skylab fell back to Earth in 1979, and some pieces landed in Western Australia.

questions.q: What is the name of China's space station?
questions.fact: Tiangong means Heavenly Palace in Chinese.

questions.q: Which reusable spacecraft did NASA fly from 1981 to 2011?
questions.fact: The Space Shuttle launched like a rocket and landed on a runway like a glider.

questions.q: Which space shuttle flew the very last shuttle mission in 2011?
questions.fact: Atlantis is now on display at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

questions.q: Which space shuttle was the first to fly into space, in 1981?
questions.fact: The shuttle Enterprise was only used for test flights in Earth's air and never went to space.

questions.q: Which space shuttle carried the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit in 1990?
questions.fact: Discovery flew more missions than any other space shuttle.

questions.q: Which space telescope, launched in 2021, sees mostly in infrared light?
questions.fact: Its main mirror is 6.5 meters wide and made of 18 hexagon-shaped pieces.

questions.q: What metal is the James Webb Space Telescope's big mirror coated with?
questions.fact: Gold reflects infrared light really well, and the coating is thinner than a human hair.

questions.q: Why does the James Webb Space Telescope have a sunshield the size of a tennis court?
choices: To keep its instruments very cold
questions.fact: Infrared telescopes must be super cold so their own heat does not blur what they see.

questions.q: Which NASA space telescope, launched in 2009, was built to find planets around other stars?
questions.fact: Kepler discovered more than 2,600 planets outside our solar system.

questions.q: What do we call a planet that orbits a star other than the Sun?
questions.fact: Scientists have confirmed thousands of exoplanets, and there are probably billions more in our galaxy.

questions.q: What is the name of the NASA rover that landed on Mars in 2021?
questions.fact: Perseverance is collecting rock samples that scientists hope to bring back to Earth someday.

questions.q: What was the name of the small helicopter that flew on Mars?
questions.fact: In 2021, Ingenuity made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet, and it went on to fly 72 times.

questions.q: Which NASA rover landed in Gale Crater on Mars in 2012?
questions.fact: Curiosity is about the size of a small car and is powered by a nuclear battery.

questions.q: What was the name of the first rover to drive on Mars, in 1997?
questions.fact: Sojourner was about the size of a microwave oven.

questions.q: Which Mars rover was planned to last 90 days but kept working for more than 14 years?
questions.fact: Opportunity drove more than 45 kilometers before a huge dust storm ended its mission in 2018.

questions.q: What is the tallest volcano in the solar system?
questions.fact: Olympus Mons on Mars is about two and a half times as tall as Mount Everest.

questions.q: What is the giant canyon system on Mars called?
questions.fact: Valles Marineris is about 4,000 kilometers long, about as wide as the United States.

questions.q: What are the names of Mars's two moons?
questions.fact: Their names come from Greek words meaning fear and dread.

questions.q: What is the largest moon in the solar system?
questions.fact: Ganymede, a moon of Jupiter, is even wider than the planet Mercury.

questions.q: Which moon has a thick hazy atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane?
questions.fact: Titan orbits Saturn, and it is the only moon with a thick atmosphere.

questions.q: Which moon is the most volcanically active place in the solar system?
questions.fact: Io, a moon of Jupiter, has hundreds of volcanoes, some shooting lava fountains many kilometers high.

questions.q: Which moon of Jupiter is thought to hide a salty ocean under its icy crust?
questions.fact: NASA's Europa Clipper spacecraft launched in 2024 to study this icy moon.

questions.q: What are Jupiter's four largest moons called as a group?
questions.fact: They are Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.

questions.q: Who discovered Jupiter's four largest moons in 1610?
questions.fact: Seeing moons circle Jupiter helped show that not everything in space circles Earth.

questions.q: Which moon of Saturn shoots jets of water ice out into space?
questions.fact: The jets come from an ocean hidden under Enceladus's icy shell.

questions.q: Which moon of Saturn has a huge crater that makes it look like the Death Star from Star Wars?
questions.fact: The giant crater is named Herschel, and it is about a third as wide as Mimas itself.

questions.q: What is Neptune's largest moon?
questions.fact: Triton orbits backward, opposite to the way Neptune spins.

questions.q: What is the name of Pluto's largest moon?
questions.fact: Charon is about half as wide as Pluto, so the two are sometimes called a double system.

questions.q: In what year was Pluto reclassified as a dwarf planet?
questions.fact: Pluto was reclassified because it shares its orbit with many other icy objects.

questions.q: In what year was Pluto discovered?
questions.fact: Pluto was spotted by comparing photos of the sky taken a few nights apart.

questions.q: Who discovered Pluto?
questions.fact: Clyde Tombaugh was 24 years old when he found Pluto at Lowell Observatory in Arizona.

questions.q: Which spacecraft flew past Pluto in 2015?
questions.fact: New Horizons found a huge heart-shaped plain of ice on Pluto.

questions.q: Who suggested the name Pluto?
questions.fact: Venetia Burney of England suggested naming it after the Roman god of the underworld.

questions.q: What is the largest object in the asteroid belt?
questions.fact: Ceres is so big and round that it is classified as a dwarf planet.

questions.q: Where is the main asteroid belt?
questions.fact: Even though it has millions of asteroids, they are spread out so far that spacecraft fly through easily.

questions.q: What is the icy region beyond Neptune, where Pluto orbits, called?
questions.fact: The Kuiper Belt is full of icy leftovers from when the solar system formed.

questions.q: What is the giant, faraway shell of icy objects thought to surround the solar system called?
questions.fact: Many comets that take thousands of years to orbit the Sun are thought to come from the Oort Cloud.

questions.q: What is a comet mostly made of?
questions.fact: Comets are often called dirty snowballs.

questions.q: Which way does a comet's tail point?
questions.fact: Sunlight and the solar wind push the tail away from the Sun, so it can even lead the comet.

questions.q: About how often does Halley's Comet come back near Earth?
questions.fact: Halley's Comet was last seen in 1986 and is due back in 2061.

questions.q: Who correctly predicted that a famous comet would return in 1758?
questions.fact: Halley died before it came back, but the comet was named after him.

questions.q: What do we call a space rock that lands on Earth's surface?
questions.fact: A meteor is the streak of light, and a meteorite is the rock that makes it to the ground.

questions.q: What causes a meteor shower?
choices: Earth passing through dust left by a comet
questions.fact: Most meteors are made by bits of dust no bigger than a grain of sand.

questions.q: Which meteor shower peaks every August?
questions.fact: The Perseids come from dust left behind by Comet Swift-Tuttle.

questions.q: What do most scientists think wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago?
questions.fact: The impact left the giant Chicxulub crater in Mexico.

questions.q: What is a black hole?
choices: An empty hole with nothing in it
A place where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape
questions.fact: Black holes form when very big stars collapse.

questions.q: What is the boundary around a black hole, past which nothing can escape, called?
questions.fact: Once anything crosses the event horizon, it can never come back out.

questions.q: What is the name of the supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way?
questions.fact: Sagittarius A* has about 4 million times the mass of the Sun.

questions.q: In what year was the first picture of a black hole shown to the world?
questions.fact: The image showed a black hole in galaxy M87, taken by a network of telescopes called the Event Horizon Telescope.

questions.q: What do we call a giant star explosion?
questions.fact: A supernova can briefly outshine its whole galaxy.

questions.q: What is a giant cloud of gas and dust in space where new stars can form?
questions.fact: The Orion Nebula is a star nursery you can see as a fuzzy spot without a telescope.

questions.q: What is a super-dense, fast-spinning dead star that sends out beams like a lighthouse?
questions.fact: The first pulsar was found in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell.

questions.q: What will the Sun swell into near the end of its life?
questions.fact: After that, the Sun will shrink into a small, hot star called a white dwarf.

questions.q: About how much longer will the Sun keep shining the way it does now?
questions.fact: The Sun is about halfway through its life.

questions.q: What color are the hottest stars?
questions.fact: Blue stars can be several times hotter than our yellow Sun.

questions.q: What color are the coolest stars?
questions.fact: Even so, the surface of a cool red star is still thousands of degrees.

questions.q: Which red supergiant star marks one shoulder of the constellation Orion?
questions.fact: Betelgeuse is so big that if it replaced the Sun, it would swallow the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.

questions.q: What is the bright blue-white star at the foot of Orion?
questions.fact: Rigel is one of the brightest stars in the night sky.

questions.q: What is the nearest big spiral galaxy to the Milky Way?
questions.fact: The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away and can be seen without a telescope on dark nights.

questions.q: What shape is the Milky Way galaxy?
questions.fact: From above, the Milky Way would look like a pinwheel with a bar of stars across its middle.

questions.q: About how long does the Sun take to circle the center of the Milky Way once?
questions.fact: The last time the Sun was in this spot in its orbit, the first dinosaurs were just appearing.

questions.q: About how old is the universe?
questions.fact: Scientists worked this out by studying the faint glow left over from the Big Bang.

questions.q: About how old is the solar system?
questions.fact: Scientists learned this partly by dating very old meteorites.

questions.q: What do scientists call the event that started the universe?
questions.fact: The name Big Bang was first used by astronomer Fred Hoyle, who did not even like the idea.

questions.q: Whose observations in 1929 showed that faraway galaxies are moving away from us?
questions.fact: This was one of the first big clues that the universe is expanding.

questions.q: Whose book, published in 1543, said that Earth goes around the Sun?
questions.fact: Before this, most people believed Earth sat still at the center of everything.

questions.q: Who worked out that planets move in oval-shaped paths called ellipses?
questions.fact: Kepler's three laws of planetary motion are still used today.

questions.q: Which planet has the shortest day?
questions.fact: Jupiter spins once in about 10 hours, even though it is the biggest planet.

questions.q: Which planet has a day that is longer than its year?
questions.fact: Venus takes about 243 Earth days to spin once but only about 225 days to orbit the Sun.

questions.q: Which of these planets spins in the opposite direction from Earth?
questions.fact: On Venus, the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.

questions.q: Which planet has the most known moons, as of 2025?
questions.fact: As of 2025, Saturn has 274 known moons, far more than any other planet.

questions.q: About how many known moons does Jupiter have, as of 2025?
questions.fact: Most of Jupiter's moons are tiny, only a few kilometers wide.

questions.q: How many moons does Mars have?
questions.fact: Both of Mars's moons are small and lumpy, like potatoes.

questions.q: Which two planets have no moons at all?
questions.fact: Mercury and Venus are so close to the Sun that a moon would be hard to keep.

questions.q: Which planet is the densest in the solar system?
questions.fact: Earth's big iron and nickel core makes it the densest planet.

questions.q: Which planet is less dense than water, so it could float in a giant enough bathtub?
questions.fact: Saturn is mostly hydrogen and helium, the two lightest elements.

questions.q: What are Saturn's rings mostly made of?
questions.fact: The pieces range from tiny grains to chunks as big as a house.

questions.q: Which of these planets also has rings, though they are very faint?
questions.fact: All four giant planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, have rings.

questions.q: How thick are most of Saturn's main rings?
questions.fact: The rings are hundreds of thousands of kilometers wide but amazingly thin, like a giant sheet of paper.

questions.q: What is the Cassini Division?
choices: A wide gap in Saturn's rings
questions.fact: It was named after astronomer Giovanni Cassini, who spotted it in 1675.

questions.q: Which planet has a giant six-sided storm pattern at its north pole?
questions.fact: Each side of Saturn's hexagon is wider than Earth.

questions.q: Which planet has the fastest winds in the solar system?
questions.fact: Winds on Neptune can blow at more than 2,000 kilometers per hour.

questions.q: Which planet was the first to be discovered with a telescope?
questions.fact: Before 1781, people only knew of the planets they could see with their eyes.

questions.q: Who discovered the planet Uranus in 1781?
questions.fact: Herschel first thought it might be a comet.

questions.q: Which planet was found by using math before anyone saw it?
questions.fact: Astronomers noticed Uranus was being tugged by something, calculated where it was, and found Neptune in 1846.

questions.q: Which planet has had the coldest temperature measured on any planet?
questions.fact: Uranus has dropped to about minus 224 degrees Celsius, even colder than Neptune, which is farther away.

questions.q: Which planet has the biggest temperature swing between day and night?
questions.fact: Mercury can reach about 430 degrees Celsius in the day and drop to about minus 180 at night.

questions.q: How long is a year on Mercury?
questions.fact: Mercury is the fastest planet, zooming around the Sun at about 47 kilometers per second.

questions.q: About how long is a year on Mars?
questions.fact: A year on Mars is almost twice as long as a year on Earth.

questions.q: About how long does Jupiter take to orbit the Sun once?
questions.fact: If you were 12 years old in Earth years, you would be about 1 in Jupiter years.

questions.q: About how long does Neptune take to orbit the Sun once?
questions.fact: Neptune finished its first full orbit since its discovery in 2011.

questions.q: About how long does Saturn take to orbit the Sun once?
questions.fact: Saturn is the farthest planet you can easily see without a telescope.

questions.q: About how long is a day on Mars?
questions.fact: From one sunrise to the next, a day on Mars lasts about 24 hours and 40 minutes, very close to an Earth day.

questions.q: What do scientists call a day on Mars?
questions.fact: Mission teams keep track of rovers by counting sols since landing.

questions.q: About how much would a person who weighs 100 pounds on Earth weigh on the Moon?
questions.fact: The Moon's gravity is about one sixth as strong as Earth's.

questions.q: On which planet would you weigh the most?
questions.fact: Jupiter's gravity at its cloud tops is about 2.4 times as strong as Earth's.

questions.q: Why do astronauts float inside the International Space Station?
choices: There is no gravity in space
They are falling around Earth along with the station
questions.fact: Gravity at the station's height is still about 90 percent as strong as on the ground.

questions.q: What is the push that sends a rocket upward called?
questions.fact: Rockets make thrust by blasting hot gas out the bottom very fast.

questions.q: Which giant rocket launched the Apollo astronauts to the Moon?
questions.fact: The Saturn V stood about 110 meters tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty.

questions.q: Which company builds the Falcon 9 rocket?
questions.fact: Falcon 9 first stages land back on Earth so they can be flown again.

questions.q: What is the name of NASA's program to send people back to the Moon?
questions.fact: In Greek myth, Artemis was the twin sister of Apollo.

questions.q: In what year did Artemis I fly around the Moon without a crew?
questions.fact: Artemis I tested NASA's giant SLS rocket and the Orion spacecraft.

questions.q: What is the name of the spacecraft that carries astronauts on NASA's Artemis missions?
questions.fact: Orion is named after one of the most famous constellations in the sky.

questions.q: What is the name of Russia's long-used crewed spacecraft?
questions.fact: Soyuz spacecraft have been carrying people to space since 1967.

questions.q: What is SpaceX's spacecraft for carrying astronauts called?
questions.fact: In 2020, Crew Dragon became the first private spacecraft to carry astronauts to the International Space Station.

questions.q: What is SpaceX's giant, fully reusable rocket called?
questions.fact: As of 2025, Starship is the largest and most powerful rocket ever flown.

questions.q: Who founded the rocket company SpaceX?
questions.fact: SpaceX was founded in 2002.

questions.q: Who founded the space company Blue Origin?
questions.fact: Blue Origin was founded in 2000, and Jeff Bezos flew to space on its New Shepard rocket in 2021.

questions.q: Which company launches thousands of Starlink internet satellites?
questions.fact: As of 2025, SpaceX has launched more satellites than any other company in history.

questions.q: Who was the first space tourist, who paid to visit the International Space Station in 2001?
questions.fact: Dennis Tito spent about eight days in space.

questions.q: Which spacecraft is the farthest human-made object from Earth?
questions.fact: As of 2025, Voyager 1 is more than 24 billion kilometers from Earth.

questions.q: What do the Voyager spacecraft carry as a message for anyone who might find them?
questions.fact: The records hold pictures, music and greetings in 55 languages.

questions.q: In what year did Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 launch?
questions.fact: Both spacecraft are still sending signals back to Earth decades later.

questions.q: Which spacecraft was the first to reach interstellar space, outside the Sun's bubble?
questions.fact: Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space in 2012.

questions.q: Which is the only spacecraft to have visited Uranus and Neptune?
questions.fact: Voyager 2 flew past Uranus in 1986 and Neptune in 1989.

questions.q: Which spacecraft orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017?
questions.fact: Cassini ended its mission by diving into Saturn on purpose.

questions.q: Which NASA spacecraft arrived at Jupiter in 2016?
questions.fact: Juno carried three small LEGO figures, including one of Galileo.

questions.q: Which spacecraft landed on a comet in 2014?
questions.fact: Philae rode on the European Rosetta spacecraft to comet 67P.

questions.q: Which probe landed on Saturn's moon Titan in 2005?
questions.fact: Huygens is still the farthest landing ever made from Earth.

questions.q: Which country's spacecraft made the first landing on the far side of the Moon, in 2019?
questions.fact: China's Chang'e 4 lander carried a rover called Yutu-2.

questions.q: Which country landed near the Moon's south pole with Chandrayaan-3 in 2023?
questions.fact: India became the first country to land near the Moon's south pole.

questions.q: Which spacecraft made the first soft landing on the Moon, in 1966?
questions.fact: The Soviet Luna 9 sent back the first pictures from the Moon's surface.

questions.q: Which spacecraft took the first pictures of the far side of the Moon, in 1959?
questions.fact: The fuzzy images showed the far side has far fewer dark plains than the near side.

questions.q: What is the name of the star pattern that looks like a big ladle or saucepan?
questions.fact: The two stars at the end of the Big Dipper's bowl point toward Polaris.

questions.q: Which constellation is known as the Hunter?
questions.fact: Orion is easy to see on winter evenings in the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.q: What are the three bright stars in a row in the middle of Orion called?
questions.fact: Following Orion's Belt to the left leads you to Sirius.

questions.q: Which constellation is shaped like the letter W or M?
questions.fact: Cassiopeia was a vain queen in Greek mythology.

questions.q: What is the Pleiades star cluster also known as?
questions.fact: The Pleiades holds hundreds of stars, but most people can see only about six or seven with their eyes.

questions.q: Which constellation is used to find south in the Southern Hemisphere?
questions.fact: The Southern Cross appears on the flags of Australia, New Zealand and Brazil.

questions.q: How many official constellations are there?
questions.fact: The International Astronomical Union set the 88 official constellations.

questions.q: Which constellation includes the North Star?
questions.fact: Polaris is the star at the end of the Little Dipper's handle, which is part of Ursa Minor.

questions.q: What does the name Ursa Major mean?
questions.fact: Ursa is the Latin word for bear.

questions.q: Which constellation is shaped like a lion?
questions.fact: Leo's brightest star is called Regulus.

questions.q: Which constellation's name means the bull?
questions.fact: The bright orange star Aldebaran marks the bull's eye.

questions.q: Which red star is called the heart of the scorpion in Scorpius?
questions.fact: Antares means rival of Mars because its red color looks like the planet.

questions.q: Which constellation is shaped like a flying swan?
questions.fact: Cygnus is also called the Northern Cross.

questions.q: Which three bright stars form the Summer Triangle?
questions.fact: The Summer Triangle is high in the sky on summer nights in the Northern Hemisphere.

questions.q: What is an asterism?
choices: A star pattern that is not an official constellation
questions.fact: The Big Dipper is an asterism that is part of the constellation Ursa Major.

questions.q: What is a binary star?
choices: A star made of computer code
Two stars that orbit each other
A star that blinks on and off
questions.fact: About half of the stars like our Sun have at least one partner star.

questions.q: Which planet is often called the Morning Star or Evening Star?
questions.fact: After the Moon, Venus is the brightest natural object in the night sky.

questions.q: What causes the auroras, like the northern lights?
choices: Particles from the Sun hitting Earth's upper air
questions.fact: The colors come from oxygen glowing green or red and nitrogen glowing blue or purple.

questions.q: What is the scientific name for the northern lights?
questions.fact: The southern lights are called the aurora australis.

questions.q: What is the solar wind?
choices: A stream of charged particles flowing out from the Sun
Wind on Earth on sunny days
questions.fact: The solar wind blows out past all the planets.

questions.q: What protects Earth from much of the solar wind?
questions.fact: Earth's magnetic field acts like an invisible shield around the planet.

questions.q: What is the giant bubble made by the solar wind around the solar system called?
questions.fact: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 have both passed through the edge of the heliosphere.

questions.q: What are the two belts of charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetic field called?
questions.fact: They were discovered in 1958 by America's first satellite, Explorer 1.

questions.q: About how far does light travel in one year?
questions.fact: That distance is called a light-year.

questions.q: What is the average distance from Earth to the Sun called when it is used as a unit?
questions.fact: One astronomical unit is about 150 million kilometers.

questions.q: About how far away is the Moon from Earth?
questions.fact: Light reflected off the Moon takes only about 1.3 seconds to reach Earth.

questions.q: How is the Moon's distance from Earth changing?
choices: It moves about 3.8 centimeters farther away each year
It moves 1 kilometer farther each year
questions.fact: Scientists measure this by bouncing lasers off mirrors left on the Moon by Apollo astronauts.

questions.q: How do most scientists think the Moon formed?
choices: From debris after a planet-sized object hit Earth
It was a comet that froze
questions.fact: The object that hit young Earth is often called Theia.

questions.q: Why can footprints on the Moon last for millions of years?
choices: The ground is made of glue
There is no wind or rain to erase them
questions.fact: Small meteorites will slowly wear them away, but it will take a very long time.

questions.q: What is the Moon phase called when we cannot see the Moon at all?
questions.fact: During a new moon, the Moon's lit side faces away from Earth.

questions.q: What is the Moon phase called when it is more than half lit but not yet full?
questions.fact: Gibbous comes from an old word meaning humped.

questions.q: What is a blue moon usually?
choices: A second full moon in one calendar month
The first full moon of winter
questions.fact: Blue moons happen about once every two to three years, which is why people say once in a blue moon.

questions.q: What is a supermoon?
choices: A moon twice its normal size
A full moon when the Moon is near its closest to Earth
A moon you can see during the day
A new moon during an eclipse
questions.fact: A supermoon looks a little bigger and brighter than an ordinary full moon.

questions.q: Which side of the Moon is often wrongly called the dark side?
questions.fact: The far side gets just as much sunlight as the side we see.

questions.q: Why does the Moon look bigger when it is near the horizon?
choices: It is a trick of the brain
It is closer to Earth then
The air magnifies it a lot
questions.fact: If you take a photo, the Moon near the horizon is the same size as when it is high in the sky.
